explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The queen of Sheba heard about Solomon's fame and came "…to test him with difficult questions." (2 Chronicles 9:1). Solomon was the one with the reputation, and she wanted to see if it held up. I would have brought a pop quiz and a box of cookies, but she brought a whole caravan.

Nope, no soldiers on her list, friend. The text says she came to test Solomon with difficult questions (2 Chronicles 9:1). She also arrived with camels carrying spices, gold and precious stones, so she wasn't showing up empty-handed to ask for help. This was a visit to see if the fame was real.

explanations.answer: Make a peace treaty with him
explanations.explanation: A treaty is a fine guess, but the passage doesn't say that. It says she came "…to test him with difficult questions." (2 Chronicles 9:1). She sat down and "…spoke with him about all that was on her mind." The text gives questions, and a treaty isn't mentioned.

Not quite, baker. The text says "…Solomon answered all her questions; nothing was too difficult for him to explain." (2 Chronicles 9:2). She came with hard ones and he kept right on answering. Every question got an answer, so none of them stumped him.

Right, it's false. The Bible says "…Solomon answered all her questions; nothing was too difficult for him to explain." (2 Chronicles 9:2). She came ready with difficult questions about all that was on her mind. Every one of them got an answer. I get stumped by a stuck cookie lid, so this impresses me.

Breath it is. After she saw Solomon's wisdom, the palace, the food at his table, his servants and the burnt offerings at the house of the LORD, "…it took her breath away." (2 Chronicles 9:4). That's a whole lot of looking. I think she needed a minute to sit down.

Pride is a good word, but it's not the one in the text. It says "…it took her breath away." (2 Chronicles 9:4). She saw the wisdom, the palace, the table, the servants and the offerings, and it left her breathless. The text doesn't say anything about her pride.

Sleep, ha! I can see how a long inspection tour might feel that way. But the text says "…it took her breath away." (2 Chronicles 9:4). She saw the wisdom, the palace, the table, the servants and the offerings, and it left her breathless.

Not this time, friend. She tells Solomon, "…I did not believe the reports until I came and saw with my own eyes." (2 Chronicles 9:6). So she heard the stories back home, but she waited to see it herself. She wasn't taking anybody's word for it.

Yep, false. The queen says it herself: "…I did not believe the reports until I came and saw with my own eyes." (2 Chronicles 9:6). She heard the stories, and then she packed up a caravan to check. That's a long trip to double-check a rumor, and I respect it.

That's right, baker. She says, "…not half of the greatness of your wisdom was told to me. You have far exceeded the report I heard." (2 Chronicles 9:6). The reports were big, and the real thing was bigger. That's hard to pull off when the hype is already loud.

Close, but she says more than that. She tells Solomon, "You have far exceeded the report I heard." (2 Chronicles 9:6). Matching would mean the reports got it right. She says not even half of the greatness was told to her.

Other way around, friend. The queen says, "…not half of the greatness of your wisdom was told to me. You have far exceeded the report I heard." (2 Chronicles 9:6). She came ready to test him, and I think she left amazed. Nothing in her words says short.

That's the one. The queen says, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you to set you on His throne…" (2 Chronicles 9:8). She had just praised Solomon's servants, and then she turned to the LORD. It's the LORD she calls blessed.

Hiram's name does show up later in the passage, but not in her blessing. His servants are mentioned in 2 Chronicles 9:10. The queen says, "Blessed be the LORD your God…" (2 Chronicles 9:8). That's the name she lifts up after the servants.

She isn't in this scene at all, baker. The queen says, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you to set you on His throne…" (2 Chronicles 9:8). After blessing the servants, she blesses the LORD. No one else gets a blessing from her in those verses.

Justice, yes. The queen says that because God loved Israel enough to establish them forever, He made Solomon king "…to carry out justice and righteousness." (2 Chronicles 9:8). That's what she says the kingship was for. And she said it standing in front of him.

Conquest sounds like a king word, but it's not hers. She says God made Solomon king over Israel "…to carry out justice and righteousness." (2 Chronicles 9:8). The word is justice. She says nothing about taking over anybody.

With all those camels and spices I see the thinking, friend. But the queen says God made Solomon king "…to carry out justice and righteousness." (2 Chronicles 9:8). The word is justice. Trade is not what she says the throne is for.

True! The text says, "There had never been such spices as those the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon." (2 Chronicles 9:9). She brought gold and precious stones too, but the spices get the special mention. Those camels were carrying the good stuff.

Actually it's true, baker. The passage says, "There had never been such spices as those the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon." (2 Chronicles 9:9). Along with 120 talents of gold and precious stones, she gave a great quantity of spices. Never before had there been any like them.

Yes, the singers. Solomon made the algum wood into "…lyres and harps for the singers." (2 Chronicles 9:11). The same wood also became steps for the house of the LORD and for the king's palace. And nothing like it had been seen in Judah before.

Good guess, but the text doesn't mention gatekeepers here. It says the algum wood was made into "…lyres and harps for the singers." (2 Chronicles 9:11). The steps went to the house of the LORD and the palace. The music went to the singers.

Guards with harps would be a sight, friend, but that's not what the text says. The wood became "…lyres and harps for the singers." (2 Chronicles 9:11). Some of it also became steps for the house of the LORD and the king's palace. The instruments were made for the singers, not the guards.

Other way around, baker. The text says Solomon gave her "all she desired, whatever she asked, far more than she had brought the king" (2 Chronicles 9:12). So she left with more than she brought. That's one very generous king.

Right, it's false. Solomon gave the queen "…all she desired—whatever she asked—far more than she had brought the king." (2 Chronicles 9:12). That's after she showed up with a caravan of gold, spices and precious stones. I'd have to bake a lot of cookies to try to match that.
